doc.title: Chico Hamilton — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: How charts were written and rehearsed in the quintet
summary: He wrote lead sheets and worked out voicing and features at rehearsal, as Duke did, and band members led rehearsals of their own tunes in a democratic way.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Well let’s go back to the quintet. Let’s say if Buddy or even if you wrote a piece and you wanted the group to play it, did you write out individual charts? How were the pieces rehearsed, how were they created?

I’d write out charts. I make a lead sheet, let’s put it like that. That’s what I do now. I make a lead sheet and I decide -- I don’t know exactly what I want voicing wise so I’ll bring it to rehearsal. We play around with it and I decide what instrument I want to use, what kind of sound I hear, who I want to feature on it. That was the hippest thing about Duke. Duke knew who to give the tune to, to play the melody, and that’s why you always identify Duke’s music with a certain instrument, you know?
So you were very democratic about it?
So if it was Buddy’s tune, he would lead that rehearsal about his tune -- as a leader?

Oh, yeah. Everybody that brought anything in, they suggested how they wanted it played. If it worked it worked, if it didn’t work, just do it over. You know, we all just decided hey, well let’s do this or let’s do that. And here again man, like I said, the only thing that could possibly change anything would be the rhythm.
